revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Puzzle Problem
revealWordProblem.text: Before a sale, a toy store's puzzle stock was 25% 300-piece puzzles, 15% 500-piece puzzles, and the rest 1,000-piece puzzles. During the sale the store sold ALL of its 300-piece and 500-piece puzzles — 120 puzzles in all. How many of each type did the store have before the sale?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The 120 puzzles sold were the 300-piece and 500-piece stock together, which is 25% + 15% = 40% of the whole stock. So 120 is the part and 40% is the percent: 0.4t = 120, giving t = 120 ÷ 0.4 = 300 puzzles in total. Now take each percent of that whole: 300-piece = 0.25 × 300 = 75, 500-piece = 0.15 × 300 = 45, and 1,000-piece = 0.6 × 300 = 180. Check: 75 + 45 = 120 sold ✓ and 75 + 45 + 180 = 300 total ✓.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — Working backwards to the whole
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. So we go up a level, not up a number: find what is always true, show it a second way, and be ready to defend it with a reason instead of an answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Percent × whole = part. When the whole is unknown, divide the part by the percent in decimal form: whole = part ÷ decimal — and you can say why it is true, and where it would stop being true.

iDo.title: Watch me find the original price of the sweater
lines: Akela paid $42 for a sweater on sale, and that was 60% of the original price. The $42 is the part; the original price is the whole, which is 100%.
On a double number line, I put $42 under 60%. To find a smaller step, I use 10%: if 60% is $42, then 10% is 42 ÷ 6 = $7.
Now I count up to the whole: 100% is ten of those 10% steps, so 10 × $7 = $70.
The equation says the same thing in one move: 0.6 × v = 42, so v = 42 ÷ 0.6 = 70. The original price was $70 — larger than the sale price, which is exactly what a discount should mean.
linesEs: Akela pagó $42 por un suéter en oferta, y eso era el 60% del precio original. Los $42 son la parte; el precio original es el entero, que es el 100%.
En una recta numérica doble, pongo $42 debajo del 60%. Para hallar un paso más pequeño, uso el 10%: si el 60% es $42, entonces el 10% es 42 ÷ 6 = $7.
Ahora cuento hasta el entero: el 100% son diez de esos pasos de 10%, así que 10 × $7 = $70.
La ecuación dice lo mismo en un solo paso: 0.6 × v = 42, así que v = 42 ÷ 0.6 = 70. El precio original era $70 — mayor que el precio de oferta, que es exactamente lo que debe significar un descuento.
iDo.titleEs: Mírame hallar el precio original del suéter

weDo.title: Try it together — then prove it
lines: Sheng's car is now worth $26,600, which is 70% of what his parents paid for it. Find the original price.
Name the pieces first: $26,600 is the part, 70% is the percent, and the purchase price is the unknown whole.
Write the percentage statement as an equation, using the decimal form: 0.7v = 26,600.
Solve by dividing both sides by 0.7: v = 26,600 ÷ 0.7 = 38,000. The car cost $38,000 when they bought it.
Now prove it: say why that move had to work at all — not just that it did.
Sentence frame — convince a skeptic: "My method works because ___ . It would stop working if ___ ."
linesEs: El carro de Sheng ahora vale $26,600, que es el 70% de lo que pagaron sus papás por él. Halla el precio original.
Nombra primero las piezas: $26,600 es la parte, 70% es el porcentaje, y el precio de compra es el entero desconocido.
Escribe el enunciado de porcentaje como una ecuación, usando la forma decimal: 0.7v = 26,600.
Resuelve dividiendo los dos lados entre 0.7: v = 26,600 ÷ 0.7 = 38,000. El carro costó $38,000 cuando lo compraron.
Ahora demuéstralo: di por qué ese paso tenía que funcionar — no solo que funcionó.
Marco de oración — convence a alguien que duda: «Mi método funciona porque ___ . Dejaría de funcionar si ___ .»

youDo.title: Now you try — and defend it
lines: Try the problems below on your own. Getting the answer is half the work — be ready to say why your method works, and where it would stop working.
Then pick one problem and show it a second way. If two different methods agree, that agreement is your proof.
linesEs: Intenta los problemas de abajo por tu cuenta. Obtener la respuesta es la mitad del trabajo — prepárate para decir por qué funciona tu método y dónde dejaría de funcionar.
Luego elige un problema y muéstralo de una segunda manera. Si dos métodos distintos coinciden, esa coincidencia es tu prueba.

conceptIntro.headingEs: Ve más allá — Trabajar al revés para hallar el entero
conceptIntro.introEs: Esto ya lo sabes hacer. Así que subimos de nivel, no de número: halla lo que siempre es cierto, muéstralo de una segunda manera y prepárate para defenderlo con una razón en lugar de una respuesta.
conceptIntro.keyIdeaEs: Porcentaje × entero = parte. Cuando el entero es desconocido, divide la parte entre el porcentaje en forma decimal: entero = parte ÷ decimal — y puedes decir por qué es cierto y dónde dejaría de serlo.

onLevel.stem: A toy store's puzzle stock was 25% 300-piece, 15% 500-piece, and the rest 1,000-piece. During a sale the store sold ALL of its 300-piece and 500-piece puzzles — 120 puzzles in total. How many of each type did the store have before the sale? Explain your reasoning.
onLevel.sampleAnswer: The 120 puzzles sold were the 300-piece and 500-piece stock together, so they represent 25% + 15% = 40% of the whole stock. That makes 120 the part and 40% the percent, with the total stock unknown: 0.4t = 120, so t = 120 ÷ 0.4 = 300 puzzles in all. Now find each type as a part of that whole: 300-piece = 0.25 × 300 = 75 puzzles, 500-piece = 0.15 × 300 = 45 puzzles, and 1,000-piece = the remaining 60% = 0.6 × 300 = 180 puzzles. Check: 75 + 45 = 120 sold ✓, and 75 + 45 + 180 = 300 ✓.
hints: What percent of the stock did the 120 sold puzzles make up?
Add the two percents before you divide.
0.4t = 120 — then use the whole to find each type.

extending.stem: A shop reports that this week's $60 in sales is 120% of last week's. Was last week better or worse, and by how much?
choices: Worse — last week was $50, so sales rose by $10
Better — last week was $72, so sales fell
Worse — last week was $48
You cannot tell without knowing the number of items sold
extending.explanation: Last week is the whole here, so last week is 100%. This week's $60 stands for 120% of last week. Divide to find the whole: 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50. Last week was $50, so sales rose by $10.
choiceFeedback: That takes 120% OF 60. Here 60 is already the 120%, so you divide rather than multiply.
That subtracts 20% of 60. The 20% is measured against last week, not this week.
The percent relationship is enough — item counts are not needed.
hints: Which number is the whole here, this week or last week?
$60 stands for 120%, so what does 100% stand for?
Divide 60 by 1.2.
extending.stemEs: Una tienda informa que los $60 de ventas de esta semana son el 120% de los de la semana pasada. ¿Fue mejor o peor la semana pasada, y por cuánto?
choicesEs: Peor — la semana pasada fue $50, así que las ventas subieron $10
Mejor — la semana pasada fue $72, así que las ventas bajaron
Peor — la semana pasada fue $48
No se puede saber sin conocer cuántos artículos se vendieron
extending.explanationEs: La semana pasada es el todo aquí, así que la semana pasada es el 100%. Los $60 de esta semana representan el 120% de la semana pasada. Divide para hallar el todo: 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50. La semana pasada fueron $50, así que las ventas subieron $10.
hintsEs: ¿Cuál número es el entero aquí, esta semana o la pasada?

extending.stem: To find the whole when $9 is 25% of it, Lena divides 9 by 0.25. Omar reasons that 25% is a quarter, so he multiplies 9 by 4. Whose method works?
choices: Both — dividing by 0.25 and multiplying by 4 are the same operation
Only Lena — multiplying cannot undo a percent
Only Omar — you should never divide by a decimal
Neither — you need the whole before you can use either method
extending.explanation: 25% is the same as one quarter. Dividing by 0.25 asks how many quarters fit into 9. Multiplying by 4 answers that same question directly. Both routes give the same whole: 9 × 4 = 36.
choiceFeedback: Multiplying by 4 undoes taking a quarter — that is exactly what is needed.
Dividing by a decimal is a normal operation and gives the same answer here.
The part and the percent are enough; the whole is what you are finding.
hints: What fraction is 25%?
Work out 9 ÷ 0.25 and 9 × 4 and compare them.
If two methods agree every time, what does that say about them?
extending.stemEs: Para hallar el entero cuando $9 es el 25% de él, Lena divide 9 entre 0.25. Omar razona que el 25% es un cuarto, así que multiplica 9 por 4. ¿El método de quién funciona?
choicesEs: Los dos — dividir entre 0.25 y multiplicar por 4 son la misma operación
Solo el de Lena — multiplicar no puede deshacer un porcentaje
Solo el de Omar — nunca se debe dividir entre un decimal
Ninguno — necesitas el entero antes de usar cualquiera de los dos métodos
extending.explanationEs: El 25% es lo mismo que un cuarto. Dividir entre 0.25 pregunta cuántos cuartos caben en 9. Multiplicar por 4 responde esa misma pregunta directamente. Los dos caminos dan el mismo todo: 9 × 4 = 36.
hintsEs: ¿Qué fracción es el 25%?
Calcula 9 ÷ 0.25 y 9 × 4 y compáralos.
Si dos métodos coinciden siempre, ¿qué dice eso de ellos?

extending.stem: To find the whole from a part and a percent, you…
choices: Divide the part by the percent in decimal form
Multiply the part by the percent
Add the part and the percent
Subtract the percent from 100
extending.explanation: Percent × whole = part, so dividing the part by the decimal undoes the multiplication and leaves the whole.
choiceFeedback: Multiplying finds a part when you already know the whole.

Subtracting from 100 finds the leftover percent, not the whole.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake when finding the whole is multiplying by the percent instead of dividing. For "$42 is 60% of the original price," computing 0.6 × 42 = $25.20 makes the original price SMALLER than the sale price — impossible for a discount. Since percent × whole = part, the whole is found by dividing: 42 ÷ 0.6 = $70. Whenever the percent is less than 100%, the whole must come out larger than the part, so a smaller answer is the tell.

connect.modelAnswerEs: Los $26,600 son la parte y el precio de compra es el entero. Escrito como ecuación, 0.7v = 26,600. Dividir los dos lados entre 0.7 da v = 38,000. El entero es mayor que la parte, lo que tiene sentido porque el 70% es menos que el 100%.
